theory.text: IELTS SPEAKING
Part 1
A step-by-step self-study guide
Understand the interview • Build natural answers • Practise short skills • Plan ideas • Complete full practice sets
This guide focuses on IELTS Speaking Part 1: the introductory interview about familiar topics such as home, study, work, daily routines, interests and preferences.
Your learning route

rows: Learn the task format, answer development, fluency, vocabulary and grammar.
Use the worked examples as reference.
Practise extending answers, choosing details, paraphrasing and correcting common errors.
Exercises E1–E9; keys at the end.
Make quick keyword plans for familiar topics without writing full answers.
Planning worksheets P1–P10; suggested plans at the end.
Answer complete sets aloud under realistic timing, then review your recording.
Compare with sample answers, explanations and self-review checklists.
All keys and sample responses are at the end.

theory.text: A study routine you can repeat

Session 1: Read one theory section and say the worked examples aloud. Session 2: Complete two or three small exercises. Session 3: plan two topics using keywords, then answer them without reading a script. Session 4: record one full practice set, review it and repeat the weakest answers.

Start untimed. Later, aim to answer each question in roughly 2–4 sentences when the question invites development. This is a practice guide, not an official requirement for a fixed number of sentences or seconds. The examiner may move on naturally; do not force every answer to the same length.

Important: sample answers are examples, not scripts to memorise. Replace the details with truthful information about your own life. IELTS assesses how you communicate in the interview, not whether your life matches the model answer.
Part 1 Theory
1. Understand the task

IELTS Speaking has three parts. Part 1 is a short interview in which the examiner asks questions about familiar topics. It normally lasts about 4–5 minutes. The questions are designed to let you talk about your life, habits, preferences and everyday experiences.

rows: What it means for your answer
Use real experiences and ordinary details; you do not need specialist knowledge.
Answer the question directly before adding a reason, detail or example.
Listen to the exact wording. A question about the past may need a past-tense answer.
Aim for clear, natural communication rather than an essay-like response.
No preparation time for each question
Develop the habit of thinking of one useful detail quickly.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Question: “Do you enjoy cooking?” A direct answer could be: “Yes, quite a lot.” A developed answer is: “Yes, quite a lot. I usually cook simple dishes at home, especially on weekends, because it helps me relax and saves money.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The answer responds immediately, then adds a routine and a reason. It does not begin with a long general statement about the importance of cooking. The details are specific enough to sound personal but easy to say.
2. Use a flexible answer pattern

A useful starting pattern is A–R–D: Answer → Reason → Detail. Add an example or contrast only when it helps. This is a planning aid, not a compulsory formula; natural answers may use two steps or reorder them.

rows: Give a clear response to the question.
Yes, usually. / Not really. / It depends. / I’d say…
mainly because… / one reason is that… / I suppose it’s because…
Add a real routine, example, place, person or contrast.
For example… / especially when… / These days… / Unlike before…

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Question: “Do you like reading?” Answer: “Yes, especially short non-fiction books. I like learning something practical without spending too much time on it, so I often read a few pages before bed.”
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Answer: yes. Reason: practical learning. Detail: short reading before bed. Each sentence adds information instead of repeating “I like reading because it is interesting.”
3. Choose the right amount of detail

A one-word answer may be understandable but gives you little opportunity to show fluency, vocabulary or grammar. At the other extreme, a long monologue can drift away from the question and create more chances for errors. A practical target is a direct answer plus one or two relevant supporting details.

rows: “Yes, I do. I usually walk in the evening because it clears my head after studying.”
“Yes, walking is important in human civilisation, and throughout history…”

theory.text: Do not add a reason when it feels unnatural or when the question simply asks for a factual detail. For “What is your hometown called?”, name the place and perhaps add a brief description. For “Why do you like it?”, explain the reason.
4. Answer the exact question

rows: Give a yes/no or qualified answer, then develop it.
Name a type or category, then give a detail.
Giving only a reason without naming anything.
State frequency, then describe a routine.
Answering only whether you enjoy it.
Give a time or period, then explain if useful.
Giving a general opinion without a time.
Name a place and describe it briefly.
Talking only about why the activity matters.
Give a reason and make it clear.
Repeating the question as the whole answer.
Talk about the past using appropriate tense.
Using present tense for a finished past experience.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Q: “How often do you use public transport?” Weak: “It’s convenient and cheap.” Better: “I use it several times a week, mainly when I go to university. It’s cheaper than taking a taxi, and I don’t have to find a parking space.”
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The improved answer begins with frequency, which is what “how often” asks for. The reasons support the answer rather than replacing it.
5. Sound natural: spoken English, not an essay

Part 1 answers should sound like thoughtful conversation. Contractions such as “I’m”, “it’s” and “don’t” are normal. Simple language is effective when it is precise. Avoid memorised openings such as “Since the dawn of time…” or “This is an intriguing question that requires deep consideration.”

rows: I think… / I’d say… / For me,…
In my humble opinion… (often overly formal)
usually / probably / more or less / I guess
Maybe, perhaps, possibly in every sentence
A long list of unrelated examples
I used to…, but these days…
Mixing past and present without a clear time change
It depends on… / If I have time,…
Using “it depends” without explaining what it depends on

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Q: “Do you often go to cafés?” Natural: “Not that often. I usually meet friends at a café once or twice a month, especially when we want somewhere quiet to chat.”
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  “Not that often” is a natural qualified answer. The frequency and situation clarify what it means. The answer is conversational without being careless.
6. Develop vocabulary through specific details

You do not need rare words for familiar topics. Choose words that describe your experience accurately. A small, useful phrase such as “a quiet neighbourhood”, “a packed schedule”, “a short commute” or “a relaxing way to unwind” can be more effective than an unnatural advanced synonym.

rows: a residential area; within walking distance; a lively neighbourhood
“I live in a fairly quiet residential area.”
meet a deadline; a practical subject; a heavy workload
“The workload gets heavy near exam week.”
unwind after class; take up a hobby; spend time outdoors
“I go cycling to unwind after class.”
keep in touch; look something up; spend time on a screen
“I use my phone to keep in touch with friends.”
home-cooked meals; a balanced diet; grab a quick bite
“I often have home-cooked meals on weekdays.”
rush-hour traffic; a reliable service; get around town
“Buses make it easier to get around town.”

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Basic: “My area is good and has many things.” More precise: “My neighbourhood is convenient because there are several cafés and grocery stores within walking distance.”
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  “Convenient” summarises the benefit, while “within walking distance” gives a concrete reason. The goal is precision, not decoration.
7. Use grammar that matches the meaning

rows: “I’m preparing for my final exams at the moment.”
“I joined a photography club last year.”
“I used to play badminton every weekend.”
be going to / plan to / hope to
“I’m planning to learn how to drive.”
usually, often, once a week, hardly ever
“I go swimming about once a week.”
prefer A to B; would rather + verb
“I prefer studying in the morning to studying late at night.”

theory.text: A useful answer can contain more than one tense when the time changes: “I used to live in a small town, but I moved to the city three years ago, and I’m much busier now.” Make the timeline clear.
8. Fluency: keep going without rushing

Fluency is not the same as speaking as fast as possible. It includes connecting ideas, maintaining a manageable pace and recovering when you need a moment to think. A brief pause is fine. Repeatedly restarting the entire sentence, filling every silence with “umm”, or speaking so quickly that words become unclear can make communication harder.
Think of one key idea, not a complete memorised sentence.
Use a short thinking phrase only when needed: “Let me think…” or “I’d say…”.
If you lose a word, explain it another way: “It’s a device you use to…”
Finish the point when you have answered the question; do not keep adding unrelated ideas.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Q: “What do you usually do at weekends?” If you cannot recall a specific activity immediately: “It depends on my workload. If I’m free, I usually meet a friend or watch a film at home. During exam periods, I tend to stay in and study.”
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  “It depends on…” gives a clear organising idea, and the two contrasting situations make the answer easy to follow.
9. Pronunciation: clarity first

Aim for intelligible speech, clear word endings and natural stress. You do not need to imitate a particular accent. Practise saying key content words clearly and grouping words into meaningful chunks. For example: “I usually take the BUS / because it’s CHEAPER / and more CONVENIENT.” Do not pause after every word.
Record yourself and check whether important words are easy to hear.
Practise word stress in useful phrases: con-VEN-ient, neigh-bour-HOOD, en-vi-ron-MENT.
Notice final sounds and plural endings: “books”, “friends”, “worked”.
Repeat a short answer with clearer chunking rather than simply speaking faster.
10. Handle common Part 1 topics
Part 1 often uses everyday topics. Prepare flexible vocabulary and real details rather than memorising a paragraph for each possible question.

rows: Where do you live? What do you like about your home? Which room do you use most?
What is your hometown like? What has changed? Would you recommend visiting it?
What do you study or do? Why did you choose it? What do you find challenging?
What is a typical day like? Are your routines different at weekends?
What do you do to relax? Did you have the same hobbies as a child?
What kind of food do you like? Do you cook? Has your diet changed?
How often do you see friends? What do you usually do together?
What device do you use most? How has technology changed your routine?
How do you usually travel? Is public transport convenient where you live?
What weather do you prefer? Does weather affect what you do?
Do you enjoy shopping? Do you prefer shopping online or in person?
What do you like reading or listening to? When do you usually do it?

theory.text: 11. Assessment criteria in practical terms

IELTS Speaking is assessed across four criteria: Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, and Pronunciation. You do not need to show every feature in every answer. Across the interview, aim to communicate clearly, connect ideas, use suitable vocabulary, vary grammar where natural and make your speech easy to understand.

rows: Answer without excessive hesitation; organise the response; avoid repetition and irrelevant detail.
Use accurate topic words and collocations; paraphrase when a word is missing; avoid forced idioms.
Control basic sentences and add a range of clauses and tenses where they fit.
Make sounds, word stress and sentence stress clear; use natural chunking and a manageable pace.

theory.text: These are study explanations, not a band-score calculator. A single answer cannot reliably determine your overall Speaking band.
12. A 10-second mental checklist
Did I answer the exact question first?
Did I add one relevant reason, detail or example?
Does my tense match the time in the question?
Are my words specific and natural?
Can the listener follow my speech without effort?

guide.text: The aim is to plan ideas, not to write a memorised speech. For each question, note only two or three keywords: your answer, one reason, and one detail. Then look away from the notes and speak naturally.

rows: Yes / no / sometimes / it depends / a specific fact: ______________________________
when / where / who with / example / past-versus-now: ______________________________
Present habit / past experience / future plan / frequency: __________________________
A precise collocation or phrase I can use naturally: ________________________________
photos of food / scenery; share with friends

guide.text: Possible spoken answer: “Yes, especially when I travel. I like taking photos because they help me capture a moment and remember the place later. I usually take pictures of scenery or food and share a few with my friends.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The notes are not complete sentences. That is intentional: they give the speaker a direction without encouraging recitation. The final answer uses connected sentences and adds grammar spontaneously.
Where do you live? What do you like about your home? Which room do you use most?
What is your hometown like? Has it changed? What would you show a visitor?
What do you study or do? Why did you choose it? What is challenging about it?
What is your morning routine? Are weekdays different from weekends?
What do you do to relax? Do you prefer staying in or going out?
What food do you like? Do you cook? Has your diet changed?
How often do you meet friends? What do you usually do together?
Which device do you use most? How does it help you?
How do you travel around your city? What would you change about transport?
What did you enjoy doing as a child? Is it different from now?
Could I answer each question directly using these notes?
Do the questions require different tenses or different kinds of information?
Are the details true for me, or have I copied a model answer?
Can I speak without reading complete sentences?
If I have no strong opinion, can I use an ordinary routine or example?

small.text: Part 2 Small exercises
Complete these tasks before checking the answer key. Say your answers aloud when the task involves speaking. The suggested times are practice estimates, not official IELTS timings.
E1. Extend a short answer
Allow 6 minutes. Add a reason and one specific detail to each answer. Do not write more than two additional sentences.
1. Q: Do you like your hometown? A: Yes, I do. →
2. Q: How often do you exercise? A: About twice a week. →
3. Q: Do you enjoy cooking? A: Not really. →
4. Q: What do you do in your free time? A: I watch films. →
5. Q: Do you use your phone a lot? A: Yes, quite a lot. →
E2. Match the answer to the question
Allow 4 minutes. Write the correct question number beside each answer.
Questions: (1) How often do you read? (2) What kind of music do you like? (3) Where do you usually study? (4) Did you enjoy sports at school? (5) Why do you use public transport?

A. “Mostly pop and acoustic music, especially when I’m travelling.”B. “Because it’s affordable, and I can avoid looking for a parking space.”C. “Usually in the library, since it’s quieter than my room.”D. “A few times a week, usually before I go to bed.”E. “Yes, I did. I played volleyball with my classmates for two years.”
E3. Improve the answer
Allow 8 minutes. Rewrite each answer so that it answers the question directly and includes relevant detail.
1. Q: How do you get to university? A: “Transport is very important in modern society.”
2. Q: What do you like about your neighbourhood? A: “It is good. It is very good and nice.”
3. Q: Did you enjoy reading as a child? A: “I like reading fantasy books now.”
4. Q: How often do you eat out? A: “Restaurants have many kinds of food, and food is necessary.”
E4. Choose precise vocabulary
Allow 5 minutes. Complete each sentence with the most suitable phrase: within walking distance • unwind • packed schedule • keep in touch • rush-hour traffic.
1. My weekdays are busy because I have a __________.
2. I usually listen to music to __________ after class.
3. There are several shops __________ of my apartment.
4. Messaging apps help me __________ with friends who live far away.
5. I leave home early to avoid the worst __________.
E5. Correct the grammar
Allow 8 minutes. Correct the error and briefly name the grammar point.
1. I am usually go to university by bus.
2. I have joined a club last year.
3. I prefer study in the morning than at night.
4. When I was a child, I use to play outside every day.
5. I enjoy to watch films with my friends.
E6. Use the right tense
Allow 6 minutes. Complete each answer using the verb in brackets.
1. Q: What do you do at weekends? A: I usually __________ (meet) friends or __________ (stay) at home.
2. Q: Did you like your school? A: Yes. I __________ (make) a lot of friends there.
3. Q: Are you learning anything new at the moment? A: I __________ (try) to improve my English pronunciation.
4. Q: Have your hobbies changed? A: I __________ (play) computer games a lot as a teenager, but now I __________ (prefer) outdoor activities.
5. Q: What are your plans for next year? A: I __________ (hope) to take an English test.
E7. Build a natural response
Allow 8 minutes. Choose one connector from the box for each gap: especially • although • so • for example • these days.
1. I like outdoor activities, __________ cycling and walking.
2. I’m quite busy with university, __________ I try to exercise at weekends.
3. I enjoy cooking, __________ when I have time to try a new recipe.
4. I used to watch television every evening. __________, I mostly watch videos online.
5. I like my neighbourhood, __________ I try to spend time outdoors.
E8. Recover when you do not know a word
Allow 6 minutes. Explain the underlined idea without using the word itself. Aim for one or two sentences.
1. “I use a thermos to keep my drink warm.” Explain what a thermos is.
2. “I enjoy gardening because it helps me relax.” Explain what gardening means.
3. “I take the underground train to work when traffic is heavy.” Explain what an underground train is.
4. “I watched a documentary about ocean life last night.” Explain what a documentary is.
E9. Spot the problem
Allow 6 minutes. Identify the main weakness in each response: off-topic, too short, repetitive, memorised/formal, or tense mismatch. Then state one improvement.
1. Q: What do you usually do after class? A: “Yes.”
2. Q: What is your hometown like? A: “My hometown is nice. It is really nice, and I think it is a nice place.”
3. Q: Did you play any sports when you were younger? A: “I play badminton every Sunday.”
4. Q: Do you enjoy shopping? A: “Since the dawn of civilisation, shopping has been a fundamental pillar of human existence.”
5. Q: How often do you cook? A: “Food is important because all humans need nutrition.”

full.text: Part 4 Full practice

Practice instructions: choose a set, start a timer or recording, and answer the questions aloud. Do not pause the recording to write. Try to keep most answers concise but developed. If you finish early, do not invent extra information; focus on clear, natural delivery.

review.text: Part 5 Complete answer key
The answers below are suggestions. Many different responses are correct if they answer the question, use appropriate grammar and sound natural. Personalise every model before practising it aloud.
Answers for E1: Extend a short answer
1. Hometown: Yes, I do. I like that it has plenty of food stalls and cafés, and most places I need are easy to reach.
2. Exercise: I exercise about twice a week, usually by cycling or doing a short workout at home. It helps me stay active when I have a lot of coursework.
3. Cooking: Not really. I can make a few simple dishes, but I usually choose meals that do not take long to prepare.
4. Free time: I watch films, especially comedies. It is an easy way to relax after studying, and sometimes I watch them with friends.
5. Phone: Yes, quite a lot. I use it to message friends, check my timetable and look up information for my classes.
Answers for E2: Match the answer
A–2; B–5; C–3; D–1; E–4. Each answer matches the information requested by its question: type, reason, location, frequency or past experience.
Answers for E3: Improve the answer
1. “I usually take the bus to university because it is affordable and the stop is close to my home.” It answers how and adds a reason.
2. “I like that my neighbourhood is quiet, and there are several grocery stores within walking distance.” It replaces vague repetition with specific detail.
3. “Yes, I did. I used to read fantasy books before bed, although I mostly read online articles now.” The answer uses past tense and can contrast with the present.
4. “I eat out about once a week, usually at the weekend when I meet friends. On weekdays, I tend to eat at home.” It answers frequency first.
Answers for E4: Precise vocabulary
1. packed schedule; 2. unwind; 3. within walking distance; 4. keep in touch; 5. rush-hour traffic.
Answers for E5: Grammar correction
1. “I usually go to university by bus.” Present simple for a routine; do not combine “am” with the base verb this way.
2. “I joined a club last year.” The finished time “last year” normally takes the past simple.
3. “I prefer studying in the morning to studying at night.” Use prefer + -ing + to + -ing, or “prefer to study … rather than …”.
4. “When I was a child, I used to play outside every day.” The expression is “used to + base verb” for a past habit.
5. “I enjoy watching films with my friends.” Use enjoy + -ing.
Answers for E6: Use the right tense
1. meet; stay. 2. made. 3. am trying. 4. played; prefer. 5. hope (or “am hoping” in a suitable context). The tense follows the time and meaning in the question.
Answers for E7: Natural response
1. for example; 2. although; 3. especially; 4. These days; 5. so. Use “especially” to single out one item or situation, not to show contrast.
Answers for E8: Explain without the word
1. “It is a container that keeps drinks hot or cold for a long time.”
2. “It means growing and looking after plants, flowers or vegetables.”
3. “It is an underground train system used to travel around a city.”
4. “It is a programme that gives factual information about real people, places, events or subjects.”
Answers for E9: Spot the problem
1. Too short / does not answer the question. Give one or two usual activities, such as having a snack or reviewing notes.
2. Repetitive and vague. Replace repeated “nice” with a concrete feature and a reason.
3. Tense mismatch. The question asks about the past; use “I played…” or “I used to play…”.
4. Memorised or overly formal. Give a direct personal answer, e.g. “Yes, especially when I need clothes or books.”
5. Off-topic. Explain how often you cook and add a routine or reason.
Suggested plans for P1–P10
P1 Home: apartment / quiet / favourite room = bedroom or study corner / future: larger place or stay nearby
P2 Hometown: city or town name / food and familiar places / new roads or buildings / visitor: local market or park
P3 Study / work: subject / reason: interest or career / challenge: workload or difficult concepts / study routine
P4 Routine: wake-up time / breakfast / commute / weekend: later start or social plans
P5 Free time: music, films, sport or games / reason: relax / prefer alone or with friends / future hobby
P6 Food: favourite dish / taste or memory / cook simple meals / diet changed because of schedule or health goals
P7 Friends: weekly or monthly / café, meal or online game / making friends: shared interests / close friends versus larger circle
P8 Technology: phone or laptop / study, messages, navigation / saves time / drawback: distraction
P9 Transport: bus, motorbike, walking or cycling / cost and convenience / service quality / improve routes or reliability
P10 Childhood: outdoor games, drawing, reading / who with / changed due to school or work / current hobby
These are keyword examples only. Your plan should reflect your own life; there is no single correct personal answer.
Model answers for full practice sets
The following models demonstrate answer length and development. They are not full scripts for memorisation. If a model does not match your circumstances, change the details.
F1. Home and accommodation
Q1 model: “I live in an apartment with my family. It is in a fairly convenient area, so shops and public transport are not too far away.”
Q2 model: “My favourite thing is that it feels comfortable and familiar. After a long day at university, it is nice to have somewhere quiet to relax.”
Q3 model: “I spend most of my time in my bedroom because I study there and keep my books and computer there. I have a small desk near the window.”
Q4 model: “Possibly. I would like to try living closer to the city centre for a while, mainly because it would make travelling around easier. However, I would still want a quiet place.”
F2. Hometown
Q1 model: “My hometown is in southern Vietnam. It is a fairly busy place, but there are also quieter residential areas.”
Q2 model: “I like the food and the fact that most people are familiar with the area. There are plenty of local places to eat, and I can usually find what I need nearby.”
Q3 model: “Yes, quite a bit. There are more shops and newer buildings than there used to be, although some older neighbourhoods have stayed much the same.”
Q4 model: “Yes, especially for someone who enjoys local food and everyday city life. I would suggest visiting a local market and trying a few regional dishes.”
F3. Study
Q1 model: “I’m studying computer engineering. It combines programming with hardware, which is what attracted me to it.”
Q2 model: “I chose it because I enjoy understanding how devices work and how software can interact with physical systems. It also gives me several possible career paths.”
Q3 model: “The most difficult part is managing several technical subjects at once. Some concepts take time to understand, so I try to practise them rather than only read notes.”
Q4 model: “I usually review the main concepts first and then solve practice questions. If I get something wrong, I try to understand why before moving to the next topic.”
F4. Daily routine
Q1 model: “I usually get up, have breakfast and check what I need to do that day. If I have an early class, I try to leave home with enough time for the journey.”
Q2 model: “I like having a rough routine because it helps me manage my time, but I do not plan every minute. I need some flexibility when assignments take longer than expected.”
Q3 model: “At weekends, I usually wake up later and have more time for hobbies or friends. During the week, most of my time is taken up by classes and coursework.”
Q4 model: “I would like to spend less time on my phone before bed. I sometimes keep scrolling longer than I intend to, so I’m trying to put it away earlier.”
F5. Free time and hobbies
Q1 model: “I usually watch films, listen to music or work on a personal project. It depends on how much coursework I have that week.”
Q2 model: “Not exactly. When I was younger, I spent more time playing games outdoors. These days, I have more screen-based hobbies, although I still enjoy going out.”
Q3 model: “I enjoy both, but it depends on the activity. I prefer doing exercise with other people, while I often watch films or study a hobby on my own.”
Q4 model: “I’d like to try photography properly. I take pictures on my phone already, but I want to learn more about composition and lighting.”
F6. Food and cooking
Q1 model: “I enjoy Vietnamese food, particularly dishes with fresh herbs and a balance of different flavours. I also like trying food from other countries when I get the chance.”
Q2 model: “I usually eat at home on weekdays because it is more affordable and convenient. I eat out when I meet friends or want to try somewhere new.”
Q3 model: “I can cook a few simple meals, such as fried rice or noodles. I’m not particularly skilled, but I can prepare something decent when I need to.”
Q4 model: “My eating habits have changed a little. I used to snack more often, but now I try to eat proper meals, especially when I have a busy study schedule.”
F7. Friends
Q1 model: “I meet my friends whenever our schedules allow, usually once a week or so. Sometimes we meet in person, and sometimes we just chat online.”
Q2 model: “We often get something to eat, visit a café or play games together. It is usually more about catching up than doing anything special.”
Q3 model: “I think it becomes easier when we have something in common, such as a class or hobby. I can be a little quiet at first, but I get more comfortable after a while.”
Q4 model: “I prefer a few close friends because I find it easier to talk openly with them. That said, it is also nice to know people from different backgrounds.”
F8. Technology
Q1 model: “I probably use my laptop the most for studying, although my phone is the device I carry everywhere. I use both almost every day.”
Q2 model: “I use it quite frequently to message people, check information and manage my schedule. I try to limit distractions when I need to concentrate on an assignment.”
Q3 model: “Definitely. I can find tutorials, share files and work with classmates online, so some tasks are much easier than they were before.”
Q4 model: “I would find it difficult to live without my phone because I use it for communication, maps and everyday information. Still, I could manage without it for a short break.”
F9. Transport
Q1 model: “I usually travel by motorbike or bus, depending on where I need to go. For short journeys, I sometimes walk if the weather is comfortable.”
Q2 model: “I prefer whichever option is more practical for the journey. A motorbike is flexible, but public transport can be less stressful when traffic is heavy.”
Q3 model: “It depends on the route. Some journeys are convenient, but waiting times and crowded vehicles can make public transport less appealing.”
Q4 model: “I think more reliable services and clearer information about routes would help. If buses arrived on time and covered more residential areas, more people might use them.”
F10. Weather and seasons
Q1 model: “I prefer warm weather with a light breeze. It is comfortable enough to go outside without feeling too cold or too hot.”
Q2 model: “Yes, to some extent. Sunny weather usually makes me feel more energetic, while several days of heavy rain can make it harder to go out.”
Q3 model: “When it rains, I tend to stay indoors, study or watch something. If I have to go out, I check the forecast and bring a raincoat.”
Q4 model: “My hometown is generally warm and humid for much of the year. Places with cooler weather feel quite different, especially in the evenings.”
F11. Shopping
Q1 model: “I do, but mostly when I need something. I’m not the kind of person who goes shopping just to pass the time.”
Q2 model: “I prefer shopping online for everyday items because it is convenient to compare prices. For clothes or electronics, though, I sometimes prefer seeing the product in person.”
Q3 model: “I usually buy food, stationery and things I need for studying. Occasionally, I buy clothes or accessories, but I try not to make unnecessary purchases.”
Q4 model: “My habits have become more planned. When I was younger, I often bought things on impulse, but now I usually compare options and think about whether I really need them.”
F12. Reading and music
Q1 model: “I enjoy reading when I find a topic that interests me. I often read online articles or practical guides rather than long novels.”
Q2 model: “I listen to a mix of pop and instrumental music. It depends on my mood, and I sometimes choose instrumental music when I need to concentrate.”
Q3 model: “I usually listen to music while travelling or doing simple tasks. I avoid it when I need to focus closely on something complicated.”
Q4 model: “Yes, I enjoyed music as a child, although I did not think much about the kinds of music I liked. I read less than I do now because schoolwork takes up more of my time.”
Self-assessment checklist

rows: I answered the exact question in my first sentence or phrase.
I added a relevant reason, routine, example or contrast.
My details were personal and plausible, not memorised.
My verb tense and frequency expressions were appropriate.
I used precise vocabulary without forcing idioms.
I spoke at a clear pace and grouped words naturally.
I avoided repeating the same idea in different words.
I could recover from a missing word by explaining it another way.
